paras.text: Publicly available datasets were analyzed in this study. This data can be found at: Repository 1: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Direct access link: https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/pisa-2022-database.html; Repository 2: Zenodo; DOI (accession number): 10.5281/zenodo.1338290.

Recent research has increasingly linked arts and broader creative participation with cognitive, social, emotional, and wellbeing-related outcomes in young people (Fancourt and Finn, 2019; Patalay and Fitzsimons, 2018; OECD, 2024). This literature has encouraged a broader view of student development beyond achievement in core academic subjects. At the same time, evidence varies by activity, design, population, and outcome, and observational associations should not be interpreted as proof that participation itself produces later change. This distinction is particularly important for large international assessments, where multiple constructs are measured within the same assessment cycle.

In 2022, PISA formally assessed creative thinking alongside its established academic domains (OECD, 2024). Barbot and Kaufman (2025) are cited for their discussion of the PISA 2022 creative-thinking assessment; their analytical sample is not used to define the present study. Here, N = 441,183 follows the study-specific inclusion rule: students from the 64 countries and economies that administered the creative-thinking assessment and had linkable student-questionnaire records meeting the analysis requirements. Longitudinal studies outside PISA have also linked sustained arts, culture, and entertainment participation with later wellbeing (Thornton et al., 2024), while performing-arts research has reported positive mental-health associations (Block et al., 2022). These findings motivate examination of psychological correlates without establishing the temporal ordering of the variables used here.

School belonging, self-regulation, and self-efficacy are theoretically relevant candidate correlates of the participation-outcome relationship. School belonging reflects students’ perceived acceptance and connection within school (Allen et al., 2021) and is associated with wellbeing and academic outcomes (Gopalan and Brady, 2020; Korpershoek et al., 2020; Štremfel et al., 2024). Self-regulation concerns the planning, monitoring, and evaluation of learning (Panadero et al., 2018) and is associated with educational performance (Tuero et al., 2022; Morosanova et al., 2023). Self-efficacy refers to beliefs about one’s capacity to carry out goal-directed actions (Bandura, 1997) and has been associated with academic success and psychological wellbeing (Schunk and DiBenedetto, 2020; Luo et al., 2023). In the present cross-sectional study, these constructs are treated as theoretically motivated intervening associations, not as temporally established mediators.

Research on arts participation and student outcomes has expanded substantially, but the evidence base varies in design, population, activity definition, and causal strength. Reviews have reported positive associations between arts engagement and academic, social, and wellbeing outcomes (Winner et al., 2013; Fancourt and Finn, 2019), while experimental and quasi-experimental studies provide stronger evidence for selected school-based interventions. Schneider and Rohmann (2021), for example, reviewed experimental and quasi-experimental arts-education studies across cognitive, social, and emotional outcomes. Other work has reported associations between arts-rich participation and academic performance (Catterall et al., 2012; Liu, 2023) and between arts education, self-efficacy, and emotional development (Su and Adenan, 2025). These literatures motivate the present model, but their findings should not be generalized automatically to the heterogeneous PISA participation index used here.

The study by Block et al. (2022) also reported that frequent performing-arts participation was associated with positive mental health in young adults, while McCrary et al. (2021) synthesized evidence on the health relevance of music and dance participation. Critical reviews nevertheless identify important limitations in the literature, including small or homogeneous samples, selective outcome reporting, short follow-up periods, and uncertainty about the psychological processes that accompany participation (Hugh-Jones et al., 2025). The present study addresses some of these limitations by using a large, heterogeneous PISA 2022 analytical sample and a common set of psychological constructs. It does not, however, assume that pooling 64 countries establishes cross-country measurement equivalence or invariant structural associations.

paras.sec_title: Music participation within the broader creative-activity measure
paras.text: Music is one of the conventional arts-related activities included in the eight-activity exposure and is the activity most directly aligned with the focus of the special issue. Music participation may involve repeated practice, attentional control, performance feedback, persistence, and mastery experiences. Ensemble participation may additionally provide opportunities for coordination, peer interaction, recognition, and school belonging. These processes overlap with the constructs examined in the present study, particularly self-regulation, self-efficacy, and belonging (Block et al., 2022; James et al., 2024; Thornton et al., 2024).

paras.sec_title: Psychological constructs: belonging, self-regulation, and self-efficacy
paras.text: School belonging is characterized as feeling valued, accepted and connected to the school environment (Allen et al., 2021). The significance of belonging has repeatedly been shown to be a major factor that impacts academic and wellbeing outcomes. Allen et al. (2021) conducted a systematic review and found that the link between school belonging and academic motivation, mental health, and decreased dropout rates are well supported by evidence from more than 200 studies. Korpershoek et al. (2020) synthesized 82 correlational studies and found consistent relationships between school belonging and motivational, social-emotional, behavioral, and academic outcomes in secondary education. A recent systematic review following PRISMA 2020 identified individual, relational, and institutional conditions associated with students’ sense of school belonging across a diverse literature (Štremfel et al., 2024). Collaborative, performative, and communal arts activities have been theorized to be associated with stronger school belonging, which may in turn be related to wellbeing.

paras.sec_title: Psychological constructs: belonging, self-regulation, and self-efficacy
paras.text: Self-regulation is defined as the ability to plan, monitor, and adjust one’s learning strategies and behaviors (Panadero et al., 2018). It has been consistently identified as one of the most powerful predictors of academic achievement across educational levels and cultural contexts (Dent and Koenka, 2016). A school-based experimental study by Tuero et al. (2022) demonstrated that training in self-regulation learning strategies produced significant short- and long-term gains in academic performance across multiple subject areas, including mathematics, sciences, and language. Morosanova et al. (2023) found, in a 3-year longitudinal study of 500 young adolescents, that conscious self-regulation functioned as a meta-resource for academic performance and psychological wellbeing during developmental transitions, with higher self-regulation consistently predicting more positive outcomes. A related empirical study by Morosanova et al. (2022) further demonstrated that conscious self-regulation, alongside motivational and personality factors, was a significant linear predictor of academic performance in school populations. The results indicate that arts programs that incorporate a systematic approach to setting goals, reflecting on experiences, and developing skills may positively impact students’ self-regulation skills, leading to benefits for students’ academic outcomes. According to Bandura (1997), self-efficacy is the person’s belief in his or her ability to engage in the behaviors required to achieve specific results and has been linked to academic performance and psychological wellbeing. Schunk and DiBenedetto (2020) found that self-efficacy beliefs were a motivational factor that accounted for academic achievement even after controlling for previous academic performance and general cognitive ability, suggesting self-efficacy’s incremental validity as a motivational construct. Based on a recent synthesis by Luo et al. (2023), academic self-efficacy could be seen as a strong predictor of learning engagement among Chinese college students, which further mediated the relationship between academic self-efficacy and academic achievement.

paras.sec_title: Psychological constructs: belonging, self-regulation, and self-efficacy
paras.text: Importantly, Jin and Ye (2022) concluded that the positive and significant relationship between fine arts education and psychological wellbeing was significantly mediated by self-efficacy and creativity among undergraduate students. Su and Adenan (2025) built on these findings by showing that self-efficacy lies on the path from visual arts education to academic performance and emotional regulation skills, and thus provides a mechanism for how arts engagement can lead to broader student outcomes. Basileo et al. (2024) found that self-efficacy played a major role in the relationships among perceived support for basic psychological needs, motivation, and academic achievement.

paras.sec_title: Creative thinking as an additional cognitive correlate
paras.text: Creative thinking is conceptually related to, but not identical with, reading literacy. PISA defines creative thinking as the capacity to generate diverse and original ideas and to evaluate and improve ideas across written, visual, social-problem-solving, and scientific-problem-solving contexts, whereas reading literacy focuses on understanding, using, evaluating, reflecting on, and engaging with texts. Participation in arts and broader creative activities may be associated with repeated ideation, experimentation, refinement, and evaluation, which provides a theoretical reason to examine creative thinking as a cognitive correlate of the participation-reading association (OECD, 2024). The substantial empirical correlation between creative thinking and reading reported in this study (r = 0.52) also means that the two constructs share meaningful variance. Creative thinking could therefore plausibly be treated as a parallel cognitive outcome in an alternative model; its placement here as an intervening variable is a theory-driven statistical specification rather than evidence that it temporally precedes reading.

All statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2023) with the following packages: lavaan (version 0.6–17) for structural equation modeling, survey (version 4.2–1) for complex survey data analysis incorporating sampling weights and design effects, semTools (version 0.5–6) for specialized SEM procedures, and psych (version 2.3.12) for reliability analysis and descriptive statistics. Data management and preliminary analyses utilized the tidyverse suite of packages. Graphics were produced using ggplot2.
